items.title: Cutting an integral into 100 trapezoids beats analytical integration for most real problems
items.claim: Most integrals appearing in physics, engineering or statistics do NOT have closed-form solutions. They're computed numerically. The simplest method (trapezoidal rule) divides the interval into strips and approximates each as a trapezoid.

options.text: Error in the trapezoidal rule is O(1/n^2) where n is the number of strips. Simpson's rule (quadratic interpolation) is O(1/n^4). Gauss-Legendre and adaptive quadrature can achieve essentially machine precision for well-behaved integrands
Always less accurate than analytical answers

items.reveal:
Trapezoidal rule: approximate integral from a to b of f(x) dx by the sum of trapezoidal strips. Error scales as h^2 (where h is the strip width), so halving h quarters the error.

Simpson's rule (uses quadratic fits to triples of points): error scales as h^4. Halving h reduces error by 16x.

For a function smooth enough on [a, b], Simpson's rule with 20 strips can give 6-7 decimal places of accuracy. Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 10 nodes can give 10-15 decimal places.

Many real-world integrals:
- integral of e^(-x^2) dx: no elementary antiderivative. Used everywhere in statistics. Always computed numerically (or via the error function erf).
- integral of sin(x)/x dx: no elementary form. Defined as the sine integral Si(x).
- integral over irregular domains, multidimensional integrals, integrals with singularities — numerical methods are standard.

Monte Carlo integration: for high-dimensional integrals (d > ~4), grid-based methods (Simpson, Gauss) suffer the 'curse of dimensionality' — n grid points per axis means n^d total. Monte Carlo (random sampling) has error O(1/sqrt(N)) independent of dimension; the standard tool for integrals in 10+ dimensions (e.g., statistical mechanics, finance).

More sophisticated: adaptive quadrature (refines where the function is wiggly), Romberg's method, Chebyshev quadrature for analytic functions, sparse grids, quasi-Monte Carlo with low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton).

The trade-off between numerical and analytical: analytical is exact when available, but unavailable for most functions. Numerical is universally applicable, with accuracy dialed up by computational cost.
items.why: Calculus class focuses on analytical integration. Real applied math is largely numerical — and the numerical methods can be vastly faster and more accurate than the analytical ones for the integrals actually needed.

items.title: A game with infinite expected payoff that no one will pay $20 to play
items.claim: Flip a fair coin. If heads, you win 2 dollars. If tails, you flip again — heads pays 4, etc. After n tails, the next heads pays 2 to the n+1 dollars. The expected payoff is infinite. People offered the game won't pay more than 10 to 20 dollars to play.
items.prompt: Why doesn't expected value match human behaviour?

options.text: Humans value money non-linearly — losing 100 dollars hurts more than the equivalent fraction of utility of gaining 100; Bernoulli proposed logarithmic utility, giving a finite expected utility despite infinite expected dollars
The game is impossible to play

items.reveal:
The expected value: (1/2)(2) + (1/4)(4) + (1/8)(8) + ... = 1 + 1 + 1 + ... = infinity. So by pure expected-value reasoning, any finite price for the game is a great deal.

Daniel Bernoulli (1738) noted that no rational person actually pays a large sum to play. He proposed that humans value money according to a logarithmic utility function, not linearly. Expected utility for the game with log utility is finite (about ln 2 plus a small constant), giving a reasonable price.

The St. Petersburg paradox launched expected utility theory (von Neumann, Morgenstern, 1944), behavioural economics (Kahneman, Tversky, 1979), and theories of risk aversion. It's one of the founding puzzles of decision theory.

It also exposes a deeper issue: the game has finite real-world payoff (the casino can't pay infinite money), so a more accurate model bounds the prize, giving a finite expected value of perhaps 20 dollars — close to what people actually pay.
items.why: Expected value is treated as the rational basis for decision-making. The St. Petersburg paradox shows it can be unbounded for games with bounded reasonable price — and that human utility is non-linear.

items.title: Compound interest of 7% turns 100 into 14,974 over 75 years
items.claim: Simple interest at 7% for 75 years: 100 + (75 x 7) = 625. Compound interest at 7% for 75 years: 100 x 1.07^75 = 14,974. The same rate, the same time. Compounding multiplies the result by 24x.
items.prompt: Why does compound interest diverge so dramatically?

options.text: Compound interest grows exponentially (multiplicatively each period); simple interest grows linearly (additively). Over long horizons, exponential growth always vastly exceeds linear, no matter the rate
The two are basically the same after enough time
Compound interest only works for whole-year periods

items.reveal_title: The rule of 72 and the magic of compounding
items.reveal:
Compound interest: each period, interest is paid on (principal + accumulated interest). Mathematically: A = P (1 + r)^n.
Simple interest: A = P (1 + r * n).

Rule of 72: at compound rate r% per year, money doubles in about 72/r years. At 7%, doubling time ~10.3 years. In 75 years that's ~7 doublings, so ~128x the original.

Applied historically: Einstein supposedly called compound interest 'the eighth wonder of the world' (apocryphal but illustrative). It explains:
- Why starting to save in your 20s vs your 40s makes such a huge difference.
- Why credit card debt at 20% APR explodes if minimum payments are made.
- Why long-run stock returns (averaging ~7% real) translate into vast wealth over careers.

For short horizons (1-2 periods), compound and simple interest are nearly equal. For long horizons, the gap is enormous. The gap is the 'magic' that financial planners try to communicate to young people, often unsuccessfully.

Negative compounding (decay) works the same way: 7% inflation halves purchasing power in ~10 years.
items.why: Linear and exponential are taught as adjacent concepts. They diverge in practice so dramatically that human intuition completely fails for long horizons. Anyone making long-term financial decisions needs to feel this in their bones.
